job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Tara Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a junior software engineer at a company in Des Moines that makes software for grain elevators, the big silos where farmers sell their crops. I studied software engineering, and my final project was an app that helps small farms track what's in each bin. Most days I fix bugs, write small features and join a stand-up at nine. I go to a small church group on Wednesdays and cook for six people on Sundays.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what's hard?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that farmers actually use the thing I build, and one of them once phoned to thank us. I don't like how tight money is. I live in a rented flat with two girls from church, I have about four days of savings, and my family runs a small hardware store that barely breaks even, so I help them rather than the other way round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, to a few friends who panicked. I'd say tools help, but the real job is knowing what customers want, and that's people work. I'd tell my church group to keep calm and keep working.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel okay about my job but not about money. The company is a decent size, but it's not rich, and entry salaries here haven't moved in two years. My loan payments are almost the same as my rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work, use the code assistant a bit more on boring tasks and ask for a raise at my first review. I'd put 60 a month aside and send 100 a month to my parents' store when they're short, as I did last year. I wouldn't change anything big.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, really. Tight, but fine. I'd rather have a small steady thing than a big uncertain thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you send money to your parents' store. How does that fit with your budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It doesn't, to be honest. I do it from what's left after rent and the loan, which sometimes means no groceries for a week. I'd rather do that than let my father close the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you tell them how tight it is for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My mother would insist I stop, and then she'd worry, and then the shop would be worse. I'd say work is going well, which is true in its way.

I'd tell my church group to keep calm.

My **loan payments** are almost the same as my rent.
do: Ask for a **raise** at my first review.
Save **60 a month** and keep sending 100 to my parents' store.
Use the code assistant more on boring tasks.
feel: **Fine but tight**, preferring a small steady thing to a big uncertain one.

fieldNote: Her anxiety is **money**: loan, rent and helping the family store.

Shows a traditional sense of family duty.

steps.text: Ask my manager for a raise at the first review
Put 60 a month into savings after rent and loan
Send 100 a month to my parents' hardware store when short
Use the code assistant for boring bug fixes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a real change, and that markets will sort it out over time, as they did with earlier machines. I'd say people who work hard and learn will do fine. I'd also say that government shouldn't rush in with rules it doesn't understand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm worried. Writing code is the first thing the card names. Our team is eight people, and I wouldn't be surprised if next year's plan has five. I'm the newest, and I know how last-in goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn to use AI tools well and take on the customer side, like visiting grain elevators and talking to farmers. I'd ask my manager if I could lead the app for small farms, since I built the first version. I'd keep my spending low and save a month of rent in the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but steady. Like waiting out a storm in the cellar. You don't like it, but you know what to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said markets will sort it out. What if they don't for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd rely on family, church and what I've saved. That's how my grandparents got through bad years, and I don't think government is the first answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first thing you'd do about being the newest on the team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the person the farmers call. If they ask for me by name, it's harder to cut me.

Government shouldn't rush in with rules it doesn't understand.
think: Writing code is the first thing the card names, and I'm the **newest** on a team of eight.

do: Learn AI tools well and take on the **customer side** with farmers.
Ask to lead the **small-farm app** I built.

fieldNote: She trusts **family and church** before government, a clear traditional line.
Plans to become hard to cut by owning customer relationships.
Honest about being the newest on a shrinking team.

steps.text: Visit grain elevators and talk to farmers every month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening, and no one's ready, and I'd say it out loud at church too. I'd tell people to look after their neighbours. I'd say politicians should stop arguing and tell us what the plan is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, my job goes. A junior software engineer is exactly what a thinking AI replaces, and the company will see that on a spreadsheet. The robots arrive three years later, which does nothing for me in 2028, and I'd have a loan and a family store to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut my spending to the bone, and ask my church for any help with food or rent if I needed it. I'd go home to my parents' town and work in the hardware store, since at least it's real work. I'd also ask a farmer I know whether he'd hire me as an assistant on his farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd feel sick, and then I'd pray, and then I'd feel sick again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd work in the store. Could it afford you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Barely. I'd work for my keep and a little more, and I'd move the store online, because I know how. It would be the one thing I could do that helps them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the company if you were let go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thank you and mean it, because they gave me my first job. And then I'd ask for a reference, and I'd ask them nicely.

say: It's **frightening**, and I'd tell people to look after their neighbours.
Politicians should stop arguing and tell us the plan.
think: A junior engineer is **exactly what** a thinking AI replaces.
The robots in 2031 do nothing for me in **2028**.

feel: **Alarmed**, feeling sick, praying, then feeling sick again.
S2.quote: I'd work for my keep and a little more, and I'd move the store online, because I know how.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose the job** and turns to family, church and farm work.

Gracious toward the employer even in the worst case.

steps.text: Cut all spending except rent, food and loan payments
Move back to my parents' town and work in their store
Ask the church about food or rent help if needed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is short, but I'd say it's a fair warning. I'd tell people to pay off debts, save, and look after their families. I'd say it's not the government's job to save every job, but it should help us learn new skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have about three years in software before it gets difficult. I'd want to be in a job where I deal with people, or in a smaller firm where I'm needed. I'd want the loan cleared before 2031, if possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the company for two years, build my farm-customer skills and pay the loan down by 200 a month. I'd also set up the hardware store online, as a side business, so that my family has an extra income. After that I'd look at a role at a farm equipment maker or a co-op, where my knowledge of farmers counts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled, I'd say. I have a mind for lists, and five years makes a decent list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a farm co-op?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because they value someone who understands both software and farming, and they move slowly. A co-op is owned by its farmers, who wouldn't fire a person for a machine without thinking twice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the risk in that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That co-ops use the same AI tools as everyone else, and so I'd just be in a different building. I'd still want some savings for that, which is why I'd keep paying the loan down.

say: Five years is a **fair warning**, so pay debts and save.
It's not government's job to save every job, but it should help people learn.
think: I'd have about **three years** in software before it gets difficult.
do: Pay the loan down **200 a month** and build farm-customer skills.
Set up the family store as an **online business**.
Look for a role at a **co-op** or farm equipment maker.
feel: **Settled**, since five years makes a decent list.
S3.quote: A co-op is owned by its farmers, who wouldn't fire a person for a machine without thinking twice.
fieldNote: She builds a plan around **farmer relationships** and the family store.

steps.text: Pay 200 a month toward the student loan
Open an online shop for my parents' hardware store
Apply to farm co-ops and equipment makers in year three
Set aside 50 a month to help my parents

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's look at AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long, and I'd say people should use it to build solid lives. I'd tell my church group to get their skills in order and keep faith in the community.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel good. I'd be 32, maybe married with a child, working in a stable role, and I'd have helped my parents' store find its feet. I'd still worry about whether the world will still want what I make, but I'd have time to change course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work and pay the loan off in five years. After that I'd save for a house, and I'd take part-time classes in agricultural technology or data work. I'd also help the store grow, because a family business with a good online presence has a real chance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. I'd think of it as having a long season to plant in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said maybe married with a child. How does AGI figure in that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quite a lot. I'd want my child to learn real skills and know their neighbours, and I'd want a house with a garden. Those things count whatever the technology does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently in the first year if you had ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say yes to more things. A new project, a farm visit, a night class. With two years I'd say no to everything except survival.

say: Ten years is long, so **build a solid life** and keep faith in the community.
I'd tell my church group to get their skills in order.
think: At 32 I'd be **married**, in a stable role, with the store on its feet.
I'd still worry about what the world will want, but I'd have time to **change course**.
do: Pay off the **loan** in five years and then save for a house.
feel: **Calm**, like having a long season to plant in.
S4.quote: With two years I'd say no to everything except survival.
fieldNote: Time lets her say **yes** to opportunities, which she links directly to calm.
Her values, home, family and community, set her priorities.
Still uneasy because her family store depends on her.

steps.text: Pay off the student loan within five years
Take evening classes in agricultural technology
Help grow my parents' hardware store online
Save a deposit for a house with a garden

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'd have no cushion, a loan and a family I'm helping, and no time to change anything. What would help is firms that tell us early, and a neighbourhood that looks out for each other, because the government alone won't.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not afraid of change, I'm afraid of change with no warning. Give me a few years and I'll manage.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of change, I'm afraid of change with no warning. Give me a few years and I'll manage.
portrait: Tara, 22, is a top software engineering graduate working at a **grain elevator software** firm in Des Moines.
She carries heavy debt, has about four days of savings and sends money to her family's hardware store.
She is traditional and steady, trusts family and church before government, and uses AI tools now and then.
Junior coding is exposed, so she plans to own **farmer relationships** and take the family store online.
She is anxious in most worlds, alarmed in 2028, and only uneasy with ten years to plan.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** scenario worries her most, with no cushion and a family store depending on her.
whatWouldHelp: Firms that give **early notice**, and a community that looks out for each other.
